Our old friend "the henteleaoh," with the uri- nating cry of "Give, give," must give pleas to this typical specimen of tho genus .11emp, who no sooner achieves hie heart's desire in one direction, than he is looking about him for some other object that may seem to in- vite his eolicitude. If he had conquered every venerable abuse, one could easily imagine his weeping thereat, like Alexan• der. But that trouble is still a long way off. Evil is Liydra-headed ; you have no sooner cut it down in one place than another phase of it stands revealed. Thus, it seems only the other day sine the old and favourite game of playing at soldiers was rendered more difficult and less exhilarating by the introduction of a new system of promo- tion. The buying and selling of commis- sions was voted a shame and a nuisance; and, despite the shrieks of many interested tt officers and gentlemen." the service was put on a new footing. We have not heard whether either the flirting or the fighting qualities for which our gallant troops are no renowned have been seriously impaired by this radical measure. And now, the turn of another branch of the national service seems to have fully come. The Church Militant has long been accustomed to dispose of her commissions to the highest bidder. "Come, who bids ?" has been the .token or understood condition of all advance to eminence in the ranks of her army. It has token many forms; from that of the vulgar and blatant exordium of the city auctioneer—who enlarges upon the small population attached to the benefice, the good society hard by, and the hunting and fishing in close proximity—to the more delicate and discriminating attention of the minister of state, who glows with gratitude of the lively sort 'towards model parsons; and the anxiety exhibited by ecclesiastical dignitaries and lay itupropontors to escape artistolic ceneui e by making provision in tem. air well as in spiritual things, " for their own household," Dlssenters and other Sehiomatics have, indeed, been in the habit of criticising this wide interpretation of the Pauline sentiment; averring that Simony was not Christian Charity, and that Nepot- ism bore small resemblance to the unselfish regard of a talent for his offspring. Pre- ciutie little they knew about itt Might they soon overcome their Philistine prijudicee, admire the rural aristocracy; and learn to be content with the ordinations of Providence and the Powers that be. But, no! the brill has been set rolling, and there is no knowing where it w,ll stip. " Purchase " with the final e is likely to be more troublesome than "Porches" without it. The latest example la furnished by the writer whose letter we re-produce to-day. Ike Sandbach " living " is, evidently, • living and something more. It fulfils all the ideal conditions of Anglican preferment. The original outlay was small ; the flub.- quent avenue large enough to satisfy any but a very ambitious descendant of the apostles. And then, how nice to be able to present the five other livings to one's brothers and sons, so disposing of the domes- tic difficulty which discounts financial sutteess in other ministerial quarters! Alas we have fallen on a sceptical age. The average taxpayer can scarcely repress the eigo of envy when he hears that the outcome of this costly religious machinery is—a good seat" in the hunting field, nice manners in the cre suet ground, and en unexceptionable "hand' at Mrs. Battle's favourite game, plat the most ordinary theological attain- ments. He positively hears without emotion that Mr. Macdona has requested the prayers of his congregation on the eve of his depar- ture on a canine mission. Ho may even go the length of wishing that the corporation which thus traffics in human souls may share the fate of other antique corruptions ; that the money-c angers may be driven igno- miniously forth from the t piritual temple which they have polluted; and that the Establishment may freon—to the infinite ad- vantage of the Church universal in these Chrietian lands—go, where its worthy re- presentative is reported to be going, "to the doge." The poor benighted citizen may be sadly lacking in that imaginadve capa- city which would, if he only possessed it, enable him to discover and admire the fit- ness of this state of things; but after all there is much to be said in his defence.
